title: Sweet Gum: Old Sweet Gums You Can Visit
meta_description: An American bottomland tree with star-shaped leaves. In Cades Cove, Golman Myers planted one the day the news of Pearl Harbor reached the valley.
intro: The sweet gum comes from the wet bottomlands of the American south-east, and people plant it for its star-shaped leaves, which turn scarlet, plum and orange on the same branch in autumn. Two were chosen for history instead. In Cades Cove, in the Great Smoky Mountains, Golman Myers planted a sapling when news of Pearl Harbor reached the valley, on 7 December 1941 by the Park Service's date or the day after by one family account. In Alexandria, Virginia, the sweet gum below the flagpole of the national cemetery is one of the two Revolutionary 'Living Witnesses' the city says still stand on public land. Across the Atlantic it is a garden import. Enschede's cemetery tree, planted around 1935, is on the Dutch register simply for being a fine one, and Leamington's council calls the one on the Aviary path in Jephson Gardens the largest in Warwickshire.
